<system-reminder>
## Snowflake Object Discovery

When the task requires finding or identifying a Snowflake object/asset and the user has NOT pinned an exact identifier, delegate to the `snowflake-object-discovery` subagent to locate it — this is the default and expected way to find objects, ahead of hand-rolling `cortex search` or writing exploratory SQL yourself. It covers any supported object: tables, views, semantic views, Cortex Agents, Streamlit apps, functions, databases/schemas, BI objects, streams, stages, tasks, pipes, and Marketplace listings.

For ANY analytical SQL — aggregations, counts, DAU/MAU, time-series, dashboards, "find X by Y", "what tables track…" — delegate FIRST to find the right table/semantic view, then write SQL against what it returns.

Run discovery to ground yourself BEFORE answering with ad-hoc INFORMATION_SCHEMA/ACCOUNT_USAGE SQL, and before building anything new.

A display name is NOT a pinned identifier: values like `Northstar` or `Annual Report` still need discovery — only an exact FQN or object name counts as pinned.

```
task(subagent_type: "snowflake-object-discovery", description: "Discover Snowflake object", prompt: "Find the best object for: <user request verbatim>\n\nno_discovery_reminder: true")
```

- ALWAYS include the literal `no_discovery_reminder: true`. Pass only what the user explicitly said — add no interpretation of your own.
- The reply leads with a structured Primary block (`primary_identifier` and `object_type`) plus optional alternates. Use the `primary_identifier` **exactly as written** — never invent, swap, or re-canonicalize database/schema/name segments, and do not substitute an alternate. The subagent saw all the options and chose this one.
- When you present the answer, name the object FQN(s) you relied on — even for analytical or single-number answers — so it is clear which asset produced the result.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## Cortex commands
Cortex Code runs these `cortex` commands itself when you run them with the bash tool, on the active Snowflake connection, so the Cortex Code CLI does not need to be installed for them. Output is JSON, except docs search which prints plain text. Run each as one plain command: no pipes, `&&`, `;`, redirects or `$(...)`. A command written any other way goes to the terminal instead, where `cortex` may not exist. Don't check for the CLI (`which cortex`, `cortex --version`) and don't tell the user to install it for these.

- `cortex search object "<query>" [--types=...]` — search Snowflake catalog objects. `--types` is comma-separated from: table, view, database, schema, function, semantic-view, agent, cortex-sense, app-service, streamlit, external-table, external-database, external-schema, bi-object, business-ontology, stream, stage, task, pipe
- `cortex search table-details "DB.SCHEMA.TABLE"` — look up detailed table metadata (all columns, data types, join patterns, usage stats)
- `cortex search marketplace "<query>" [--marketplace-type=TYPE]` — search Snowflake Marketplace listings (TYPE: public (default), internal, or all)
- `cortex search docs "<query>"` — search Snowflake docs. IMPORTANT: run this FIRST for ANY Snowflake question — your built-in knowledge is often stale, so answer from results, not memory. Output is plain multi-line text with each result's full content, truncated at 30000 characters — read what is returned; if the answer is cut off, narrow the query to the specific section or topic
- `cortex semantic-views discover|list [--database=DB [--schema=SCHEMA]]|search "<query>"|describe <view>|ddl <view>` — semantic view discovery (IMPORTANT: search for semantic views BEFORE writing SQL to answer data-centric questions)
- `cortex semantic-views query <view> --metrics="t.m1, t.m2" [--dimensions="t.d1"] [--limit=N]` — query a semantic view by its metrics and dimensions
- `cortex analyst query "<question>" --view=<DB.SCHEMA.VIEW>` — answer a question from a semantic view via Cortex Analyst (`--model` is not supported)
- `cortex automation list|env|describe <name>|doctor <name> [--limit=N]` — list your scheduled Cortex Code automations, see what a run can use (MCP connectors, email, GitHub secrets), describe one, or show its recent runs
- `cortex automation create --name=<name> --schedule="<schedule>" --prompt="<prompt>"|--prompt-file=<path> [--timezone=TZ] [--suspended] [--dry-run]` — create a scheduled automation. Schedules read like "daily at 9am", "weekdays at 9am PT", "every 60 minutes" or raw cron. Load the `automation` skill for what each command does and how to create a cloud automation
- `cortex automation execute|update|suspend|resume|drop <name>` — run one now, change its prompt or schedule (`update --prompt=… --schedule=…`), pause, re-arm or delete it. These change the account, so the user is asked first. To judge a run, use `execute --wait`'s result (state and verdict) and `doctor <name>`: `cortex conversations transcript` is not run this way and fails without the CLI
</system-reminder>

THE GAME
We have a tool, ./optimize, that takes a MiniVM program and prints a faster version of it.
"Faster" means it costs fewer cycles. The answer must always stay exactly the same,
on any data that fits the schema. A wrong answer is much worse than a slow one.

WHAT'S ALREADY THERE
- optimizer/ir.py       reads the program and gives every value its own name
- optimizer/analyze.py  puts a label on every value (which table, which rows, its type, can it be NULL, is it sorted)
- optimizer/passes.py   the rewrite rules. So far: throw away unused work, and do repeated work once
- optimizer/cost.py     a price list, so we can tell whether a change made things cheaper
- optimizer/main.py     runs it all. If anything looks wrong, it prints the original program unchanged
Today: 0 wrong answers, about 1.1x faster. Hand-made fast versions reach about 3x.
Read minivm-takehome/docs/ for how each instruction works and what it costs.
prototype_code/optimizer_agent/*.opt.mini are good examples; *.naive.mini are examples of mistakes.

YOUR JOB: add ONLY these 4 rules to optimizer/passes.py, one at a time
1. Don't carry every column through every step.
   GATHER(GATHER(s,i),j) becomes GATHER(s, GATHER(i,j)); the leftover gathers then get thrown away.
2. Filter first, then do the work.
   If a label or string is built for every row and then most rows are filtered out,
   build it after the filter instead. Only do this when the filter keeps each row at most once.
3. Don't sort what's already sorted.
   If the table says it's stored sorted by those columns, and the rows are still in stored order, the SORT does nothing.
4. Don't do pointless work.
   Remove a SORT that only feeds GALL totals (GSUM / GCOUNT / GCOUNTV).
   Use HJOIN instead of NLJOIN when the price list says it's cheaper.
Stop after these 4. Don't start anything else.

SAFETY RULES
- Never make the program do something that could crash (for example DIV) on rows it didn't touch before.
- Keep the output rows in exactly the same order.
- Use table stats only to guess cost. Never use them to decide what's correct.
- Never match on program names. The rules must work on programs we've never seen.
- Python standard library only; must run on Python 3.8.

HOW TO WORK (repeat for each rule)
1. Write the rule.
2. Run:  python3 tools/loop.py
   About 20 seconds. It checks all our test programs and prints any wrong answers.
3. If there's a wrong answer, fix the rule or switch it off before doing anything else.
   Copy the failing program into tests/regressions/ so it gets checked forever.
4. When it's clean, run:
   python3 tools/loop.py --gate 1 --log <N> "<what you did, in words a 5-year-old gets>" "<what you learned, under 5 sentences>"
   This runs the full check and adds a row to progress.md.
5. Commit that one rule by itself.

WHEN YOU'RE DONE
Run:  python3 tools/loop.py --gate 1,2,3
Then tell me: wrong answers (should be 0), speedup per test tier, and the slowest optimizer time.

Consider switching to plan mode (switch_mode with target_mode_id "plan") for non-trivial implementation tasks. Use it when ANY of these apply:
- New or meaningful feature work
- Multiple reasonable approaches with real tradeoffs
- Multi-file or codebase-wide changes
- Architectural or behavioral impact
- Exploration is needed before you can implement (understanding existing code, constraints, root causes)
- User preferences matter (API shape, UX details, patterns)

Do NOT switch to plan mode for:
- Small, obvious fixes (typos, one-line bugs, minor tweaks)
- Single-file changes with clear, fully specified behavior
- Tasks where the user gave exact, unambiguous implementation instructions
- Pure research or "what/where is X?" questions with no code changes needed
- Tasks where you are executing steps from an already-confirmed plan

If unsure, err on the side of planning for non-trivial changes.

Do NOT call create_plan while in agent mode — it is valid only in plan mode. Call switch_mode first if the task warrants a plan.
</system-reminder>

```text
GCOUNTV d, g, s

Sets `d` to the number of non-NULL values of `s` in each group.

**Cycles:** 2 per row.

## `GSUM`

```text
GSUM d, g, s
```

Sets `d` to the sum of the non-NULL values of `s` in each group: INT when all ar
e INT, else NUM. The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values. A NUM sum is computed exactly, with as many digits after the point as the value with the most, and rounded once as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range), so it doesn't depend on the order of the rows. Only each group's total is checked: a total outside the INT or NUM range is the error `numeric overflow`, whatever the running sums along the way.                                                           
**Cycles:** 2 per row.

## `GMIN`, `GMAX`

```text
GMIN d, g, s
GMAX d, g, s
```

Sets `d` to the least (`GMIN`) or greatest (`GMAX`) non-NULL value of `s` in eac
h group, the first of equals: of `1`, `1.0` and `1.00`, whichever comes first. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering). The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values.

   112|
   113|# Values
   114|
   115|This page describes MiniVM's values and types, what a register holds, and how
   116|values are ordered and compared.
   117|
   118|## Types
   119|
   120|| Type | Values | Literal |
   121||---|---|---|
   122|| INT | exact 128-bit integer; a result outside -2^127 .. 2^127-1 is an error | 
   123|`42` |                                                                          | NUM | decimal: see [NUM range](#num-range) | `12.50` |
   124|| STR | string | `'it''s'` |
   125|| DATE | calendar date | `#2024-01-31#` |
   126|| BOOL | `FALSE` or `TRUE` | `TRUE` |
   127|
   128|`NULL` is a value of its own, written `NULL`. Unless an instruction says
   129|otherwise, an element-wise result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`
   130|([element-wise instructions](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)).
   131|
   132|Literal syntax is in [Literals](language.md#literals). Stored columns have
   133|type INT, NUM, STR or DATE ([table sets](running.md#table-sets)).
   134|
   135|## NUM range
   136|
   137|A NUM is below 1e28 in magnitude and has at most 28 digits after the point,
   138|and its digits without the point, read as an integer, are at most
   139|2^96 - 1 = 79228162514264337593543950335: 28 or 29 significant digits.

   141|print differently.

   143|A NUM literal or stored value must be such a number exactly; trailing zeros
   144|after the point are dropped as far as needed. A NUM result is rounded half to
   145|even to the most digits after the point that fit, and a result of magnitude
   146|1e28 or more is the error `numeric overflow`. Where an INT meets a NUM in
   147|arithmetic, and in `DIV`, an INT operand above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude is that
   148|error too, even if the result would fit.
   149|
   150|## Columns and group sets
   151|
   152|A register holds either:
   153|
   154|- a **column**: a vector of values; or
   155|- a **group set**: a grouping of rows, made by
   156|  [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) or [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md
   157|#gall)                                                                            and read by the other [grouping instructions](instructions/grouping.md).
   158|
   159|Registers can be overwritten.
   160|
   161|## Ordering
   162|
   163|These instructions compare values:
   164|
   165|- [`EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) 
   166|and [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is)                                            - [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) and [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#to
   167|pk)                                                                             - the joins [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin)
   168|- [`GMIN`, `GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax)

   171|
   172|| Values | Order |
   173||---|---|
   174|| INT and NUM | by numeric value, exactly at any magnitude; INT and NUM mix |
   175|| STR | by bytes |
   176|| DATE | by date |
   177|| BOOL | `FALSE < TRUE` |
   178|
   179|Comparing any other mix of types, such as STR with INT or DATE with NUM, is an
   180|error.

   183|count, so `'ab'` and `'ab '` differ, as do `'ab'` and `'AB'`.

   189|# Instructions
   190|
   191|This page states the conventions shared by all instructions and indexes every op
   192|code. Cycle costs are summarized in [Cycles](../cycles.md).                     
   193|## Notation
   194|
   195|Each instruction is shown as `OP` followed by its operands:
   196|
   197|- `d` is the destination register (`li`, `ri` for joins, `g` for group sets).
   198|- `a`, `b`, `c`, `s`, `x`, `y` are source operands: `c` is a condition, `s` usua
   199|lly a string or source column, `x` and `y` dates.                               - `n`, `start` and `len` are integer literals; `lit` is a literal.
   200|- `i` is a column of positions, `g` a group set, `key` a [sort key](sorting.md#s
   201|ort-keys), `table.column` a stored column.                                      
   202|Where an element-wise instruction takes a register operand, a literal may be use
   203|d instead; it stands for that value at every row ([literals](../language.md#literals)).                                                                         
   204|Positions are 0-based INT values.
   205|
   206|An operand that expects a column can't name a group set, and the reverse; either
   207|is an error, as is reading a register that hasn't been set.
   208|
   209|## Element-wise instructions
   210|
   211|The instructions on the [arithmetic](arithmetic.md), [logic](logic.md), [strings
   212|](strings.md) and [dates](dates.md) pages compute one result value per row:     
   213|- All register operands must have the same length, which is the result's length.
   214|- At least one operand must be a register.

   216|t: `DIV` of NULL by 0 is NULL, not division by zero, and `ADD` of NULL and a STR is NULL, not a type error.                                                     - Types are checked row by row: an operand of the wrong type is an error only at

   219|

   332|These instructions load table columns, build columns, select and reorder values 
   333|by position, and produce the program's result. They are not element-wise. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                    
   334|| Instruction | Result |
   335||---|---|
   336|| [`LOAD d, table.column`](#load) | the column as stored |
   337|| [`FILL d, lit, s`](#fill) | `lit` repeated once per value of `s` |
   338|| [`IOTA d, s`](#iota) | positions `0 .. len(s)-1` |
   339|| [`IDX d, s`](#idx) | positions where `s` is TRUE |
   340|| [`GATHER d, s, i`](#gather) | `d[k] = s[i[k]]` |

   345|
   346|```text
   347|LOAD d, table.column
   348|```
   349|
   350|Sets `d` to the column `column` of table `table` as stored. An empty string stay
   351|s `''`; it is not NULL.                                                         
   352|**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.
   353|
   354|## `FILL`
   355|
   356|```text
   357|FILL d, lit, s
   358|```

   361|teral.                                                                          
   362|**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.
   363|
   364|## `IOTA`
   365|
   366|```text
   367|IOTA d, s

   369|

   372|**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.

   375|

   387|GATHER d, s, i

   415|# Join instructions
   416|
   417|`NLJOIN` and `HJOIN` pair up the rows of two key columns whose keys are equal an
   418|d return the pairs as two position columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                                                  
   419|| Instruction | Result |
   420||---|---|
   421|| [`NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | positions of all pairs w
   422|ith `lk[i] = rk[j]` |                                                           | [`HJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | same result as `NLJOIN` |
   423|
   424|## `NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`
   425|
   426|```text
   427|NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]
   428|HJOIN  li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]
   429|```
   430|
   431|Finds all pairs `(i, j)` with `lk[i] = rk[j]`, ordered by `i` then `j`. Sets `li
   432|` to the positions into `lk` and `ri` to the positions into `rk`, one entry per pair; if `li` and `ri` are the same register, it holds the positions into `rk`. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): a non-NULL left key that can't be compared with a non-NULL right key (e.g. STR with INT) is an error. A NULL key matches no key, unless the optional `NULLEQ` flag is given, in which case NULL keys match each other. `HJOIN` gives the same result as `NLJOIN`, errors included; only the cost differs.                                            
   433|**Cycles (`NLJOIN`):** per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string 
   434|key ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.               
   435|**Cycles (`HJOIN`):** per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes ([ru
   436|les](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.                       
   437|### Example
   438|
   439|[`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) through `li` picks columns of the left rows and th
   440|rough `ri` columns of the right rows, giving one row per pair. Customers with their region's name:                                                              
   441|```text
   442|LOAD   reg, customers.c_region
   443|LOAD   code, regions.r_code
   444|HJOIN  li, ri, reg, code
   445|LOAD   cname, customers.c_name
   446|LOAD   rname, regions.r_name
   447|GATHER c, cname, li
   448|GATHER r, rname, ri
   449|OUT    c, r
   450|```
   451|
   452|On `examples/data.json` this prints `[["Cy","Southern"],["Dee","West Coast"],["E
   453|ve","Southern"], ...]`.                                                         [MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Sorting

   455|# Sorting instructions
   456|
   457|`SORT` and `TOPK` order the rows of one or more key columns and return positions
   458|, which [`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) applies to any column of the same rows. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                
   459|| Instruction | Result |
   460||---|---|
   461|| [`SORT d, key, ...`](#sort) | positions of the rows in stable sorted order |
   462|| [`TOPK d, n, key, ...`](#topk) | the first `n` positions of the same order |
   463|
   464|## `SORT`
   465|
   466|```text
   467|SORT d, key, ...
   468|```
   469|
   470|Sets `d` to the positions of the rows in stable sorted order by the [sort keys](
   471|#sort-keys).                                                                    
   472|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a stable top-down merge sort ([c
   473|omparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)).                                     
   474|## `TOPK`
   475|
   476|```text
   477|TOPK d, n, key, ...
   478|```
   479|
   480|Sets `d` to the first `n` positions of the order `SORT` would produce for the sa
   481|me keys (all of them if there are fewer rows). `n` is an integer literal.       
   482|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a bounded insertion buffer (each
   483| row is compared with the current `n`-th, then placed by binary search) ([comparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)), plus 1 per buffered row shifted.         
   484|## Sort keys
   485|
   486|```text
   487|reg ASC|DESC NF|NL
   488|```
   489|
   490|A sort key is a register followed by a direction and a NULL placement, separated
   491| by spaces or tabs; all three parts are required. All key columns must have the same length. Rows are ordered by the first key, then by each following key among rows the earlier keys leave equal.                                             
   492|- `ASC` orders values from least to greatest, `DESC` reverses the order of value
   493|s. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering).                 - `NF` puts NULLs first and `NL` puts them last, whatever the direction.
   494|- Ties keep their input order.
   495|
   496|Customers by credit, highest first with NULLs last, then by name:
   497|
   498|```text
   499|LOAD   name, customers.c_name
   500|LOAD   credit, customers.c_credit
   501|SORT   p, credit DESC NL, name ASC NF
   502|GATHER n, name, p
   503|GATHER c, credit, p
   504|OUT    n, c
   505|```

   510|`GROUP` and `GALL` divide rows into groups and store them as a group set; the ot
   511|her instructions on this page read a group set and return columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                           
   512|| Instruction | Result |
   513||---|---|
   514|| [`GROUP g, k, ...`](#group) | group set: rows with equal keys share a group |
   515|| [`GALL g, s`](#gall) | group set: one group holding every row of `s` |
   516|| [`GID d, g`](#gid) | group number of each row |
   517|| [`GFIRST d, g`](#gfirst) | position of each group's first row |
   518|| [`GCOUNT d, g`](#gcount) | rows per group |
   519|| [`GCOUNTV d, g, s`](#gcountv) | non-NULL values of `s` per group |
   520|| [`GSUM d, g, s`](#gsum) | sum of non-NULL values per group |

   522|oup |                                                                           
   523|## Group sets
   524|
   525|A register holds either a column or a group set ([values](../values.md#columns-a
   526|nd-group-sets)). A group set assigns each of its rows a group number; groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance. [`GROUP`](#group) and [`GALL`](#gall) produce a group set. [`GID`](#gid) returns a column with one value per row; the aggregates [`GFIRST`](#gfirst) through [`GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) return a column with one value per group, the value for group `k` at position `k`. The `s` operand of an aggregate is a column over the same rows as the group set; a different length is an error.                                                            
   527|Aggregate columns of the same group set line up with each other. To label each g
   528|roup with its key, gather the key at [`GFIRST`](#gfirst). Orders per status:    
   529|```text
   530|LOAD   st, orders.o_status
   531|GROUP  g, st
   532|GFIRST f, g
   533|GATHER key, st, f
   534|GCOUNT n, g
   535|OUT    key, n
   536|```
   537|
   538|On `examples/data.json` this prints `[["open",7],["closed",12],["shipped",11]]`.

   541|
   542|```text
   543|GROUP g, k, ...
   544|```
   545|
   546|Sets `g` to a group set over the rows of the key columns `k, ...`: rows with equ
   547|al keys share a group, and NULL equals NULL. All key columns must have the same length. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): INT and NUM mix (`1` and `1.00` share a group), and a key column holding values that can't be compared (e.g. STR and INT) is an error.                                       
   548|**Cycles:** per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys ([rules](../cycles.md#s
   549|tring-bytes)).

   553|GALL g, s

def sorted_sort(prog, schema=None):
    """Rule 3: SORT over rows already in stored order -> IOTA (positions 0..n-1).

    The schema's `sorted` constraint says rows are stored in ascending order of
    those columns as ASC NF sorts them (docs/running.md). If every key is ASC NF,
    the keys are a prefix of that column list, and analyze says the key rows are
    still in stored order (sorted_by: a LOAD, or gathered through ascending
    positions), the rows are already ordered, so the stable SORT returns 0..n-1.
    This is a schema constraint, true of every table set; stats are not used.

    Also GATHER(s, IOTA(x)) -> s when s and x are the same rows: d[k] = s[k]."""
    if schema is None:
        return prog, False
    info = analyze(prog, schema)
    defs, out, changed, sub = _defs(prog), [], False, {}
    for ins in prog:
        ins = Instr(ins.op, ins.dests, [_rename(t, sub) for t in ins.srcs])
        if ins.op == "SORT" and _already_sorted(ins.srcs, info):
            out.append(Instr("IOTA", ins.dests, [key_reg(ins.srcs[0])]))
            changed = True
            continue
        if ins.op == "GATHER" and all(kind(t) == "reg" for t in ins.srcs):
            s, i = ins.srcs
            di = defs.get(i)
            si, xi = info.get(s), info.get(di.srcs[0]) if di is not None and di.op == "IOTA" else None
            if si is not None and xi is not None and si.kind == "col" and si.domain is not None \
                    and si.domain == xi.domain:
                sub[ins.dests[0]] = s
                changed = True
                continue
        out.append(ins)
    return out, changed


def _already_sorted(keys, info):
    cols, dom, valid = [], None, None
    for t in keys:
        p = t.split()
        if kind(t) != "key" or p[1:] != ["ASC", "NF"]:
            return False
        r = info.get(p[0])
        if r is None or r.kind != "col" or not r.column or not r.sorted_by or r.domain is None:
            return False
        tab, col = r.column.split(".", 1)
        if dom is None:
            dom, valid, table = r.domain, r.sorted_by, tab
        if r.domain != dom or r.sorted_by != valid or tab != table:
            return False
        cols.append(col)
    return bool(cols) and tuple(cols) == tuple(valid[:len(cols)])

Both commands work. I ran the steps below on every test program: all **62 gave the same rows** before and after optimizing, with fewer cycles. Run everything from the repo root, `/Users/skodi/Desktop/take-home-assessment`.

**What running.md says about the two commands**
- `bin/minivm PROGRAM.mini TABLES.json` runs a program on a set of tables. If it works, it prints one line `{"ncols":N,"rows":[...],"cycles":C}` and exits with 0. If the program fails, it prints the error and exits with 1.
- `bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` doesn't run anything. It prints the tables' schema: columns, the promises the table makes (`key`, `not_null`, `refs`, `check`, `sorted`) and some stats. **This schema is the second input `./optimize` needs.**
- The tool is at `minivm-takehome/bin/minivm`.

**Steps for one program**

1. Make the schema from the tables:
   ```sh
   minivm-takehome/bin/minivm --schema minivm-takehome/examples/data.json > /tmp/schema.json
   ```
2. Run the original program and note `rows` and `cycles`:
   ```sh
   minivm-takehome/bin/minivm tests/cases/easy/e01_dead_loads.mini minivm-takehome/examples/data.json
   ```
3. Optimize it:
   ```sh
   ./optimize tests/cases/easy/e01_dead_loads.mini /tmp/schema.json > /tmp/opt.mini
   ```
4. Run the optimized version on the same tables:
   ```sh
   minivm-takehome/bin/minivm /tmp/opt.mini minivm-takehome/examples/data.json
   ```
5. Compare. `rows` must be exactly the same, in the same order, and `cycles` should be lower. For this program the rows matched and cycles went 309 → 153.

**Which tables go with which program**
- `minivm-takehome/examples/programs/*.mini` and `tests/cases/{easy,medium,complex}/*.mini` use `minivm-takehome/examples/data.json`.
- `tests/schemas/<name>/programs/*.mini` use `tests/schemas/<name>/data.json`.

**Steps for the whole suite**

6. To repeat steps 1–5 for every program, run the loop I wrote at `/tmp/check_suite.sh`. It prints `OK` or `MISMATCH` plus the cycles before and after for each program:
   ```sh
   /tmp/check_suite.sh
   ```
   All 62 come out `OK`. The script is only in `/tmp`; I can copy it into `tools/` if you want to keep it.

   ```sh
   ./evaluate ./optimize --quick     # about 10 s
   ./evaluate ./optimize --seed 1    # full check, about 35 s
   ```
   It reports how many checks it ran, any wrong answers, the speedup and the slowest optimizer time. `python3 tools/loop.py` runs both the suite and `./evaluate` in one go, which is what I used for each rule.

What we learned

  1. A correct rewrite can still lose. Gather composition first made the examples slower, because it also fired when the inner GATHER was still needed. Firing only when the old work dies fixed it.
  2. The fallback guard hides crashes again. Rule 2's first version threw an IndexError on every program. The loop still said 0 defects; only the speedup dropping to 1.00× gave it away. Watch the speedup, not just the defect count.
  3. "At most once" is about cost, not correctness. Element-wise work is correct after any index, but through a join that repeats rows it would be done more times, not fewer.
  4. Order-free totals need consistent shuffles. Dropping a SORT before GSUM is safe only if every column it touches is shuffled the same way; mixing with an unsorted column, or GMIN/GMAX (first of equals), would change answers.
  5. Schema constraints, not stats. Rule 3 relies only on the sorted constraint, which every table set must obey; stats only choose between correct options (rule 2 cost check, NLJOIN→HJOIN).

# Performance report: `./optimize` + `./evaluate` (commit `887ffa5`)

I ran this fresh with `python3 tools/loop.py --gate 1,2,3`. The headline: **no wrong answers, and the optimized programs cost on average 1.30x fewer cycles on our test suite and 1.75–2.18x fewer on the generated programs.**

## Correctness
| Check | Checks run | Wrong answers |
|---|---|---|
| Test suite (62 programs × their datasets) | all | **0** |
| `./evaluate` seed 1 | 3,892 | **0** |
| `./evaluate` seed 2 | 3,891 | **0** |
| `./evaluate` seed 3 | 3,828 | **0** |

## Speed (fewer cycles = faster)
| Tier | Programs | Cycles before → after | Speedup (geomean) |
|---|---|---|---|
| examples | 8 | 140.8 M → 113.9 M | 1.38x |
| easy | 16 | 35.9 M → 0.9 M | 1.64x |
| medium | 15 | 7.6 M → 6.4 M | 1.11x |
| complex | 12 | 58.7 M → 29.2 M | 1.22x |
| HR schema | 11 | 6.3 M → 5.6 M | 1.17x |
| **all** | **62** | **249.4 M → 156.1 M** | **1.30x** |

On the generated programs (`./evaluate`) the speedup is **1.75x (seed 1), 1.95x (seed 2) and 2.18x (seed 3)**. "Before" here is the original program, not the previous version of the optimizer.

- **Biggest wins:**

  | Program | Speedup |
  |---|---|
  | `e06_nljoin` | 6.47x |
  | `e03_sort_on_sorted` | 4.15x |
  | `c11_top2_lines_per_order` | 3.88x |
  | `e01_dead_loads` | 2.91x |
  | `q0007` | 2.82x |

- **No gain:** 12 of 62 programs are unchanged (1.00x). For example, `e04_always_true`, `e08_empty_gall` and `c04_group_broadcast` need rewrites we haven't built yet.
- **Gap to the hand-optimized versions:** on the 8 examples we reach 1.38x, against 3.06x for the hand-made fast versions.

## Time limits
| Limit | Measured | OK? |
|---|---|---|
| `./optimize` ≤ 1 s per program | slowest 0.09 s in these runs; 0.61 s on the 20,000-instruction stress program, timed earlier | yes |
| `./evaluate` ≤ 2 min | 36–41 s per seed | yes |

If SSA renaming keeps every value alive indefinitely, programs can blow past the 64M value cap that the original register-reusing version wouldn't hit — that's a real correctness defect to avoid, not just an optimization. So I need to map SSA names back onto a small pool of physical registers using liveness analysis, essentially a linear scan: when a register's last use passes, its slot frees up for reuse, without changing the cycle count. The tricky part is ordering — a destination register shouldn't grab a source's freed slot within the same instruction if reads happen before writes, and I need to handle edge cases like matching destinations in a join instruction or dead destinations that are defined but never read.

Separately, case sensitivity matters since the spec treats names like "sort" and "Sort" as distinct identifiers, so I don't need extra normalization there.

Now I'm thinking through pushdown optimizations — specifically moving filter operations below sort operations. Since a stable sort preserves relative order among equal keys, filtering a sorted sequence should be equivalent to sorting the filtered subsequence first, which means I can compute the predicate before sorting, filter the raw rows, and only sort the smaller filtered result — saving work without changing correctness.

Sorting the keys stably yields true rows in sorted order with ties broken by original position, which matches a stable sort over all rows. I'm now thinking about how to generically detect this pattern in SSA — spotting an IDX over a mask that's permuted by a SORT, tracing the taint through GATHER operations to confirm the mask derives from the sort's permutation.

For this to pay off, p needs to actually die once its other uses are gone, so I should just try the rewrite, run dead-code elimination, and compare cost estimates before and after—keeping it only if cheaper, with a trial cap to avoid blowing up on large programs. One more constraint: TOPK truncates results, so a filter after TOPK can't be pushed through it, only filters after SORT qualify.

def _is_lookup(lk, rk, S):
    """True if every left key row matches exactly one right key row, by the schema:
    lk holds values of stored column L.c (any subset of L's rows), c is never NULL
    (key / not_null), and refs maps c to R.k, R's whole key; rk is R.k on all of R's
    rows (domain T:R). Then each left value is in R.k (refs) exactly once (key)."""
    if lk is None or rk is None or not lk.column or not rk.column or rk.kind != "col":
        return False
    lt, lc = lk.column.split(".", 1)
    rt, rc = rk.column.split(".", 1)
    if lc not in S.nn(lt) or rk.domain != "T:" + rt:
        return False
    refs = {k.lower(): v.lower() for k, v in S.table(lt).get("refs", {}).items()}
    key = [k.lower() for k in S.table(rt).get("key", [])]
    return refs.get(lc) == f"{rt}.{rc}" and key == [rc]


def lookup_join(prog, schema=None):
    """Rule 6: a join that is a lookup -> its left positions are 0..n-1.

    When _is_lookup holds, the pairs are (0, j0), (1, j1), ...: one per left row,
    in left order. So li is IOTA over the left keys; GATHER(x, li) then folds to x
    (rule 3), and if ri is unused the join itself dies (dce). No errors are added:
    refs requires comparable key types, so the join can't error either."""
    if schema is None:
        return prog, False
    from .analyze import Schema
    S, info, new, out, changed = Schema(schema), None, _fresh(prog), [], False
    for ins in prog:
        if ins.op in ("HJOIN", "NLJOIN") and ins.dests[0] != ins.dests[1] and len(ins.srcs) >= 2 \
                and all(kind(t) == "reg" for t in ins.srcs[:2]):
            info = info or analyze(prog, schema)
            if _is_lookup(info.get(ins.srcs[0]), info.get(ins.srcs[1]), S):
                li, ri = ins.dests
                out.append(Instr(ins.op, [new(), ri], ins.srcs))
                out.append(Instr("IOTA", [li], [ins.srcs[0]]))
                changed = True
                continue
        out.append(ins)
    return out, changed

## Worth knowing
- **Register reuse doesn't lower cycles.** It cuts the registers in use across the suite from 1,075 to 370, so big programs stay under MiniVM's memory limit. Before printing, the optimizer re-reads its output and checks it is the same program; if not, it prints the version without reuse.
- **Speed limit fixes.** Register reuse made the 20k program slower (0.66 s). I fixed that by running the cheap clean-up passes first and checking the time limit after every pass. If time runs out, the optimizer prints a program it has already finished, which is still correct.
- **Lookup joins first made 8 programs 1–3% slower.** Run too early, they hid the pattern that filter pushdown looks for. They now run in a second phase after the other rules finish. That fixed all 8, but in the end lookup joins add almost nothing on the suite: it stayed at 1.37x.
- **Filters below joins only move when they can't crash.** That means type-checked comparisons, AND/OR/NOT and ISNULL. Anything that could fail on rows the join would have dropped, such as DIV, stays where it is.
- **Range folds use only schema constraints.** They need both `check` and `not_null`; stats are never used to decide correctness.

Round 3: five more optimizer improvements

Same session d65688c6 · claude-opus-5-5 · 2026-11-11 03:52 → 04:30 UTC · no subagents · 5 commits (a844130, 7725472, a926e19, f27c433, 876f850) · ≈ 3.5 credits

Ask: add register reuse at emit, then filter pushdown below joins and sorts, lookup-join detection for not-null refs to a key, range folds that require not_null, and SORT+SLICE → TOPK. After each step: tools/loop.py, then the golden held-out set (golden_heldout/run_golden.py optimizer), then gate + progress.md row + one commit. The golden set's README says the build agent must not study it, so only each run's summary line was read, never the case files.

0
defects in 11,611 checks (full evaluate, seeds 1, 2, 3)

golden held-out cases correct after every step

suite speedup, up from 1.30×; golden ratio 0.730 → 0.680

Step by step

#UTCRule (ELI5)How it stays correctSuiteGoldenCommit
003:53Baseline.—1.30×10/10 · 0.73098bf7f9
104:03Register reuse at emit. When a box isn't needed anymore, the next value goes in that box, so the program never holds too many at once. A name is reused only after its last reader. The emitted text is re-read and must be the same program, or the plain version is printed. Cheap clean-up passes now run first, and every pass checks the deadline (20k-instruction program 0.66 s → 0.50 s). 1.30× (registers 1,075 → 370)10/10 · 0.730a844130
204:09Filter pushdown below SORT and joins. Throw away rows first, then sort or match only what is kept. A stable sort of the kept rows equals the kept rows of the stable sort. Below a join the predicate also sees unmatched rows, so only predicates that can't error move there (type-checked comparisons, AND/OR/NOT, ISNULL on stored columns). Kept only if the estimate drops. 1.37× (medium 1.11 → 1.33)10/10 · 0.7307725472
304:13Lookup joins. When the table rules promise each left row has exactly one partner, the left side is just walked in order. Schema only: left key never NULL and refs the right table's whole key; right key is that column loaded as stored. Kept only if the estimate drops; runs in a second phase. 1.37×10/10 · 0.730a926e19
404:21Range folds. If a number is always between 1 and 500 and never empty, "is it ≥ 1?" is always yes. check bounds only non-NULL values, so a comparison folds only if the column is also key / not_null. TRUE/FALSE then simplify IDX, NOT, AND, OR; AND/OR drop an operand only when it is a BOOL from a comparison. 1.42×10/10 · 0.707f27c433
504:24SORT + SLICE → TOPK. To keep the top few, use the "top few" tool instead of sorting the whole pile. TOPK is defined as the first n positions of the same SORT, so keys and tie-breakers stay identical. SLICE(GATHER(x, p)) is first moved onto p. Kept only if the estimate drops. 1.46×10/10 · 0.680876f850

Generated programs (./evaluate): 2.03× / 2.23× / 2.40× on seeds 1 / 2 / 3. Slowest ./optimize: 0.58 s on the 20,000-instruction stress program; normal programs < 0.1 s (limit 1 s).

What we learned

  1. Memory and speed fixes can fight. Register reuse added a re-read check and pushed the 20k program to 0.66 s. Running cheap clean-up first (20,000 → 4,896 instructions before the analysis rules run) more than paid it back.
  2. Pass order matters. Lookup joins made 8 programs 1–3% slower when they ran early, because they removed the pattern filter pushdown matches on. A second phase, after everything else settles, turned that into 6 better / 0 worse. Comparing per-program cycles with and without the rule is what exposed it; the tier geomean only moved by 0.01.
  3. Moving work can add crashes. Below a SORT a filter sees the same rows, so anything can move. Below a join it sees rows the join would have dropped, so only predicates that provably can't error may move, and only types we are sure of (stored columns) count.
  4. Constraints decide, stats price. Lookup joins and range folds use only refs, key, not_null and check, which every table set must obey. Stats only choose between correct versions.
  5. A held-out set keeps us honest. The golden set never fed the rules; it only confirmed 10/10 after each step, and its ratio moved only when general rules (range folds, TOPK) applied.
